topic: The Science of Refraction: Why Light Bends
target_audience: High school students or introductory physics learners

sections.title: The Optical Illusion: The 'Broken' Pencil
lecture_lines: A fox sees a fish deep in the pond.
Light from the fish bends at the water's surface.
This creates an illusion, making the fish appear shallower.
animations: Draw a horizontal water surface (#1E90FF) with a fox icon (#D2691E) above and a fish icon (#FFD700) below.
Animate a light ray (#FFFF00) traveling from the fish to the surface and bending toward the fox's eye.
Draw a dashed ray (#FFFF00, opacity 0.5) extending straight back from the eye to a shallow, 'apparent' fish.

sections.title: Prerequisite Knowledge: Speed and Optical Density
lecture_lines: Light travels faster through air than through dense glass.
We see light slow down as it enters glass.
The index of refraction calculates this speed change.
animations: Show two light pulses (#FFFFFF) starting at the same x-position in Air (top) and Glass [Asset: /mmfs1/data/home/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/glass.svg] (bottom, #E0FFFF).
The pulses move right; the pulse in Glass moves significantly slower than the one in Air.
Display the formula 'n = c / v' (#FFFFFF) and highlight the speed 'v' (#00FF00) as the pulses finish.

sections.title: The Mechanism: The 'Shopping Cart' Analogy
lecture_lines: A shopping cart moves smoothly across the paved sidewalk.
One front wheel hits the grass and slows down.
This imbalance causes the entire cart to pivot.
The cart now travels at a sharper new angle.
Light waves bend exactly like this angled shopping cart.
animations: Top-down view: A rectangular cart (#808080) with 4 wheels (#333333) moves diagonally on pavement (#AAAAAA).
The front-right wheel enters a green grass patch (#228B22), turns red (#FF0000), and slows down.
The cart's body rotates towards the grass side as the remaining wheels continue at original speed.
The cart continues through the grass at a steeper angle relative to the boundary normal.
Fade out cart; show parallel wave fronts (#FFFFFF) hitting the boundary and pivoting exactly like the cart.

sections.title: The Math: Snell's Law and Geometry
lecture_lines: Consider the boundary between air and dense glass.
A light ray hits the boundary near the normal.
Entering the glass, the ray bends toward the normal.
Snell's Law mathematically predicts this change in direction.
We measure these angles relative to the perpendicular normal.
animations: Draw a horizontal air-glass boundary (#FFFFFF); label Air (n=1.0) and Glass (n=1.5, #E0FFFF).
A red laser ray [Asset: /mmfs1/data/home/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/laser.svg] (#FF0000) strikes the boundary; add a vertical dashed Normal line (#FFFFFF).
The ray bends toward the Normal inside the glass; label the Incident and Refracted angles.
Display Snell's Law: n1 * sin(theta1) = n2 * sin(theta2) (#FFFFFF) and color-code n1 and n2.
Overlay a semi-transparent protractor (#FFFFE0) to show the angle of refraction is smaller than the angle of incidence.

sections.title: The Principle of Least Time: Fermat’s Logic
lecture_lines: A lifeguard must reach a swimmer as fast as possible.
Multiple paths exist, but only one is the fastest.
The optimal path involves more running and less swimming.
This path minimizes total travel time to the swimmer.
Light follows Fermat’s Principle, taking the path of least time.
animations: Top half: Sand (#F4A460), Bottom half: Water (#1E90FF). Place Lifeguard at point A and Swimmer at point B.
Show three candidate paths: a straight line, a refracted-like path, and a 'too wide' path.
Highlight the refracted-like path (more sand travel, less water travel) in bright green (#00FF00).
Animate the lifeguard moving along all paths simultaneously; the green path reaches the swimmer first.
Label the green path 'Principle of Least Time' (#FFFFFF) and fade out the other sub-optimal paths.

sections.title: Extreme Bending: Total Internal Reflection
lecture_lines: Light inside glass hits the boundary at steep angles.
At the critical angle, light can no longer escape.
Total internal reflection keeps data trapped inside fiber cables.
animations: A light source inside a glass block (#E0FFFF) emits rays at increasing angles toward the air boundary.
As the angle increases, the refracted ray bends closer to the surface until it hits 90 degrees (Critical Angle).
Increase the angle further; the ray reflects perfectly back into the glass; show a pulse bouncing in a fiber optic cable (#FFFFFF) [Asset: /mmfs1/data/home/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/fiber.svg].

sections.title: Summary and Synthesis
lecture_lines: Lenses use refraction to focus light into sharp images.
Total internal reflection gives diamonds their brilliant sparkle.
Understanding refraction helps the fox finally catch the fish.
animations: Show a convex lens (#E0FFFF) focusing incoming parallel light rays (#FFFFFF) to a single point.
Transition to a diamond shape (#B9F2FF) with internal light rays (#FFFFFF) reflecting and exiting with sparkle effects.

Final scene: The fox [Asset: /mmfs1/data/home/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/fox.svg] (#D2691E) from Section 1 aims lower than the apparent fish [Asset: /mmfs1/data/home/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/fish.svg] and successfully grabs it.
